title: Robust many-body quantum batteries
authors: Finn Schmolke, Karen Hovhannisyan, Milton Aguilar
abstract: Realistic work extraction from many-body quantum batteries must be local. However, only a small fraction of energy eigenstates of a generic many-body system, called scars, can support local extraction. The remaining bulk is useless for the task due to the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Here we devise a universal low-complexity protocol that steers any initial state towards exactly one scar---representing a charged state of the battery---from which a macroscopic amount of work can be extracted using local unitary operations. This is achieved by leveraging the nontrivial interplay of engineered dissipation and continuous indirect measurement that, in addition, leads to enhanced stability and charging speed compared to any other strategy using these processes independently. Moreover, the protocol works directly on the hardware level, in that it requires no simulation or suppression of interactions between subsystems. Our construction thereby enables macroscopic charge storage in steady states of generic nonintegrable many-body systems indefinitely, from which a reliable stream of work can be extracted via purely local means.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, low-complexity protocol to extract macroscopic work from quantum batteries modeled by nonintegrable many-body systems. It achieves this by using a combination of engineered dissipation and continuous measurement to force the system into a rare, stable 'scar' state. This method bypasses the limitations imposed by the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis, offering a pathway for reliable quantum energy storage.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a reliable, local method to extract macroscopic amounts of work from large, strongly interacting quantum systems (quantum batteries) whose bulk eigenstates are useless due to thermalization.
main_result: The authors propose a combined protocol using engineered dissipation and continuous indirect measurement to steer the system into a rare, non-thermal 'scar' state, enabling sustained, local work extraction.
method: The protocol is derived using quantum stochastic differential equations, combining engineered Lindblad dissipation with measurement backaction to drive the system to a specific, stable steady state.
model_or_system: The study focuses on generic nonintegrable many-body systems, exemplified by the spin-1 XY chain Hamiltonian. The key resource is the 'scar' state, which is a specific, non-thermal eigenstate.
key_observables: Local ergotropy (extractable work), average charging time, and the time-integrated measurement current used for scar certification.
important_parameters: The protocol's performance is analyzed across various coupling regimes and depends on the structure of the underlying algebra (e.g., su(2)).
main_assumptions: The protocol is assumed to work directly on hardware, requiring no simulation or suppression of interactions between subsystems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four stages of the process (discharged to work extraction), compare the charging time of the proposed protocol against alternatives, and show the time-integrated measurement current for state certification.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical limitation (ETH bulk vs. local work). It then details the combined protocol (dissipation + measurement) to reach a scar state. Finally, it optimizes the local unitaries to calculate the maximum extractable work from the resulting scar state.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics and energy harvesting in complex quantum matter, providing a concrete, hardware-implementable mechanism for energy storage in interacting quantum systems.
